clue.text: Outdated Alf due to be replaced

indicators.note: the letters of ALF DUE are to be put back in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone called Alf is old-fashioned and ripe for replacement.
explanation.walkthrough: Alf reads as a man's name, but he is only three letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Feudal describes the medieval system of lords and vassals, so it is used loosely for anything hopelessly out of date.

clue.text: Less tethering around dog

indicators.note: the letters are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: A dog is kept on a looser leash than before.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog is literally less tethered in the surface, which is apt: an English setter is a gundog bred to range freely.
explanation.definitionFit: The English setter is a long-haired breed of gundog.

clue.text: Abandons the trenches

blocks.note: to ditch something is to abandon it
long narrow channels dug in the ground, the noun sense

explanation.surface: A soldier deserts the front line in wartime.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about desertion; split it after the verb and each half means DITCHES.
explanation.definitionFit: Ditch is both a verb for abandoning and a noun for a long narrow trench.

clue.text: Some articulate feelings about librarian's penalty

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are used

explanation.surface: Someone speaks eloquently about how they feel about a library fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the word break in the middle of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A late fee is the charge a library makes when a book is returned after its due date.

clue.text: Stout carrier

blocks.note: the noun: a dark, strong beer, not the adjective for fat
someone paid to carry luggage at a station or hotel

explanation.walkthrough: Stout looks like an adjective meaning fat, qualifying carrier; here it is the noun, a dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Porter is a dark beer and also someone paid to carry bags.

clue.text: Each year, Rose loses nothing – analyse that

blocks.note: per annum, the abbreviation for each year

explanation.surface: A rose that never fails to bloom year after year invites the reader to work out why.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is O, the zero shape. Rose looks like a flower or a verb, but it is just four letters to trim.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from grammar: breaking a sentence into its parts and naming each one's role is analysing it.

clue.text: Religious man cut tail off bunny

indicators.note: a word's tail is its end, so docking the tail of bunny's word removes its final letter

explanation.surface: A cleric docks a pet rabbit's tail.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunny is the source word RABBIT, and the cut is one letter at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish religious teacher and leader.

clue.text: Learning to manipulate thin gentlemen

indicators.note: the letters are to be worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is taught how to push skinny gents around.
explanation.walkthrough: Learning here is the noun for knowledge gained, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Enlightenment is understanding or insight, the state that learning brings.

clue.text: Troublemaker got tiara smashed

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A troublemaker has broken a tiara.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the answer neatly: smashing a tiara is just what a troublemaker would do.
explanation.definitionFit: An agitator stirs up unrest, which is making trouble.

clue.text: Bishop, advanced in years, is fearless

blocks.note: B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: An elderly bishop is described as brave.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make it read as a description of the bishop; in fact the bishop gives one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bold means brave, unafraid.

clue.text: Shortly sense sound of disappointment

indicators.note: the word is cut short by its final letter

blocks.note: SIGHT, a sense, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone soon picks up a disappointed noise.
explanation.walkthrough: Shortly looks like it means soon; here it means the next word is shortened. Sense is SIGHT, one of the five senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A sigh is the long breath let out in disappointment.

clue.text: Charge to sling out emotions

indicators.note: the letters of SLING are put out of order

explanation.surface: Someone is told to fling out their emotions.
explanation.walkthrough: Sling out reads as a phrasal verb meaning throw away; sling is really the fodder and out the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the surface's emotions are the things a person feels.

clue.text: Decent teas put out after church

indicators.note: the letters of TEAS are put out of place
the rearranged letters come after CH

blocks.note: CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: Proper cups of tea are served once the church service ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Put out reads as served; here it is the signal to scramble TEAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste means pure and modest, which is decent in the moral sense.

clue.text: I get in trouble but make light of it

indicators.note: GET IN is thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone lands in hot water but laughs it off.
explanation.walkthrough: Make light of it usually means shrug something off; read literally, it means set it alight. In here is part of the fodder, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom read literally: making light of something normally means treating it as trivial, but taken word for word it means setting it alight.

clue.text: Make angry scene in broadcast

indicators.note: the letters are scattered, like seed broadcast over a field

explanation.surface: Something shown on air stirs up anger.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadcast reads as television; its older sense is to scatter seed widely.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb, stressed on the second syllable, unlike the noun for burnt perfume.

clue.text: Perfect beginners

blocks.note: the surface pushes flawless; the setter means complete or utter, as in a perfect stranger
people just starting out, so the whole phrase means total newcomers

explanation.walkthrough: Perfect reads as flawless, which beginners rarely are; here it means complete, as in perfect strangers.
explanation.definitionFit: Novices are people new to an activity, total beginners.

clue.text: Airtight solution of the crime

indicators.note: the letters are worked out into a new order

explanation.surface: A detective's explanation of a crime leaves no gaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Airtight suggests a watertight case; solution suggests solving the case, but it signals a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Hermetic means sealed so that no air can get in or out.

clue.text: Parent covered in bandages?

blocks.note: a mother, in the British childish word
an embalmed Egyptian body, wrapped in linen strips

explanation.surface: A mother is swathed in dressings after an accident.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second definition is playful: a mummy is not literally someone wearing bandages.
explanation.definitionFit: Mummy is a mother, and also an embalmed body wrapped in cloth.

clue.text: Swim with alien back to warm

indicators.note: the joined letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a dip is a quick swim

explanation.surface: A dip with an extraterrestrial helps someone warm up again.
explanation.walkthrough: Back to warm reads as warming up again; back is really the reversal and warm alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tepid means lukewarm, only slightly warm.

clue.text: Contend with inclusion of new plant

indicators.note: VIE has N included inside it

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to get a new plant accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes between the I and the E of VIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A vine is a climbing plant, especially the grapevine.

clue.text: The way to get 'em to check

explanation.surface: Advice on the best method for bringing people under control.
explanation.walkthrough: Get is part of the surface's phrasing and 'em supplies EM. Check is a verb here, as in check the flow.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: you stem bleeding or a tide of complaints just as you check them, by holding them back.

clue.text: Experienced sudden fear when dad was arrested

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
nicked is British slang for arrested by police

explanation.surface: Someone was terrified when their father was taken in by police.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, to be nicked is to be arrested.
explanation.definitionFit: To panic is to experience sudden overwhelming fear.

clue.text: Spoke loudly and harshly of the hair feature, reportedly

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so use the sound

blocks.note: a braid is a plait of hair

explanation.surface: Someone loudly criticised another person's hairstyle.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoke harshly of reads as criticised; here of simply links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To bray is to make a donkey's harsh cry, or to speak or laugh loudly and harshly.

clue.text: Substitute keepers at zoo enclosure

indicators.note: the answer is enclosed within the next words

explanation.surface: Stand-in keepers are working at the zoo's enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: Enclosure fits the zoo scene so well that it reads as a pen; it signals letters enclosed in the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz means substitute, usually an inferior imitation.
